title: Coding Adventure: Ray Tracing
subject: CS / graphics
beats: Sets out to experiment with ray tracing; names the book and blog he learned from
Builds inside a game engine so the built-in renderer is a baseline to compare against
Draws a grid of points on the camera's projection plane; checks it tracks FOV and rotation
Walks the code: plane height from FOV and trig, grid transformed by the camera
Draws arrows for the rays shot from the camera
Real light flows from the sun to the eye; we go backwards, ancient Greek style, because it's cheaper
Millions of rays: a manager script sends camera data to a GPU shader
Shader basics: return red, then x and y coordinates as gradients
Ray struct; outputs direction as color and checks axes map to RGB
Next baby step: spheres as pure math instead of triangles
Sphere equation; solve for distance; discriminant decides miss, touch or two hits
hitInfo struct; normal vector means 'which way is up on the surface'
Tests one sphere white on black: 'seems pretty spherical'
Many spheres: loop over all, keep the closest hit; checks depth order
Smooth surfaces reflect at equal angles (specular); rough ones scatter (diffuse)
Plays at inventing a random number generator from overflowing multiplies
First attempt looks patterned; tries more; then swaps in tested code from online
Random direction: sample a cube until inside a sphere, then normalize
Gets stuck in a while-true loop and crashes the computer; adds a loop limit
Shows skipping the rejection step clumps points at cube corners
Normal distribution trick works 'for maths reasons I haven't yet grasped'
Flip directions outside the hemisphere using the dot product with the normal
Trace loop: hit, move to hit point, bounce randomly, until limit or miss
Ray color multiplies by object color, like a black object absorbing all light
Track incoming light separately; emissive materials add light tinted by the path
Core shader: seed, camera ray, trace
Renders a 'photorealistic room without light'; adds a glowing ball as a sun
Bounce limit 1, 2, 30: indirect light appears, extra bounces matter less
Noise comes from one ray per pixel; average 100 rays
Too slow; accumulate over frames so the image improves over time
Missed rays gather a simple sky gradient with a sun disc
A slanted beam spreads over more area, so it should count less
Cosine weighting via the dot product; before/after comparison
Compares with the built-in renderer to notice contact shadows and color bleed
Cosine-weighted bounce directions give the same result faster, 'maths I don't understand'
Triangles: one triangle first, then a 456-triangle chess knight
Triangle and mesh buffers; same closest-hit logic as spheres, plus bounding boxes
Cornell box with colored walls; the knight emerges with colored bounce light
1, 2, 10 bounces compared; Suzanne the monkey poses
An optimization breaks Suzanne; reverts it
Specular reflection via the reflect function; blend by smoothness
Four balls at smoothness 0.4 to 1: blurry to crisp mirror
Mirrored balls and a hall-of-mirrors knight room
Why are a red tomato's highlights white, when ours are tinted red?
A clear coating reflects some light untinted; same for varnished wood
Specular probability per material picks coating vs diffuse bounces
The tomato ball now looks tomato-y
Depth of field: focus on a single pixel's rays
Random point in a circle; without the square root, points cluster in the middle
Code doesn't compile; looks up matrix syntax
Blur everything; bonus: a tiny blur gives anti-aliasing
Offset ray origins instead so rays converge on a focal plane
Test scene: shift focus between pawns, knight, king and queen
Glass, volumetrics and performance left for later

meta.notation_note: Code appears early (1:46) but each piece of math (sphere equation, dot products) arrives only when the next visual step needs it. Viewers are rarely asked questions; the presenter asks himself.
meta.misconception: yes: 2:26 (light goes from source to eye, so tracing backwards seems wrong); 29:57 tomato highlights
meta.brute_force: yes, often: home-made RNG (9:00), cube rejection sampling (11:14), no-sqrt circle points (32:43), shown and then replaced
meta.examples: many scenes: spheres, Cornell box knight, Suzanne, mirror balls, tomato, chess depth of field
meta.examples_grow: grows in complexity: one sphere, many spheres, triangles, meshes, materials, camera effects
